The sock showed a slower wind speed more closely aligned with runway XX. The three point landing was normal but very soon after touch down the plane started to turn to the right. Crosswind control settings did not correct the deviation and the right turn tightened to a ground loop. We stopped facing the opposite direction with the left wheel off the runway. Upon further inspection, the landing gear was still fully functional so we received permission from the tower to taxi back to the hangar with the safety vehicle following just in case we needed it. Lesson learned, I have always told myself that if a directional deviation began while landing to simply add power to reject the landing and go around. For some reason my mind was set that I had landed and I could recover from the tightening turn.Also, if a second runway is available and more closely aligned with the wind then take it. No award is handed out for handling a crosswind in a tailwheel aircraft.
ASRSN:2112787.s: The pilot landed a tailwheel aircraft on runway XX despite a reported 10-knot crosswind, resulting in a ground loop to the right after touchdown. The deviation tightened despite control inputs, leaving the aircraft facing the opposite direction with the left wheel off the runway, though the gear remained functional for a taxi back.

ASRSN:2112803.n: After entering lower ceilings than forecasted I asked for a pop up IFR clearance. Shortly after entering IMC I found myself in a 30 degree bank and realized it was safer to stay in marginal VFR. I had flown 4 hrs and 30 mins that day with some time in IMC. I recognize I need more practice to fly in marginal conditions especially after a long flight. I have contacted my CFII and we are going to make sure I am proficient in IMC conditions before I fly in Marginal VFR conditions without an experienced IFR pilot with me. I should have made the safer decision to stay at ZZZ. I will make better decisions going forward. I am thankful for the help of ATC and Tower controllers.
ASRSN:2112803.s: A pilot entered IMC after lower-than-forecasted ceilings and experienced a 30-degree bank while requesting a pop-up IFR clearance. The pilot attributed the incident to fatigue and insufficient IMC proficiency, deciding to remain in marginal VFR and commit to further training.

ASRSN:2112832.n: My student was pilot flying, I was giving IFR instruction. Upon rollout on the last landing of the flight returning back to ZZZ, I looked back and noticed a Piper PA28 rolling out behind us that I heard in the pattern earlier. I immediately took control and exited the runway as the plane was catching up to us. He was behind us in the pattern, we made every call, the last call I remember he made was entering base for runway XX. He had to have been within 50 feet of us on the runway and as we exited I called him on the radio to ask if he saw us and he said yes he sees us and continued to roll out. After exiting the plane I attempted to find the person flying the Piper to check what was going on and offer him a lesson on runway incursions, but he was nowhere to be found and his aircraft was already tied down.
ASRSN:2112832.s: An IFR instructor and student pilot exited the runway immediately after noticing a Piper PA28 rolling out dangerously close behind them during rollout at ZZZ. The Piper pilot, who had reported entering base, admitted seeing the aircraft but continued his rollout, resulting in a near collision within 50 feet.

ASRSN:2112848.n: Just had bought brand new micro drone DJI mini 3. Was at home performing test flight of basic drone controls from ground to my balcony and drone was outdoors operating in class B airspace. I had thought I was under a class B shelf but later realized I was still within the boundaries. Flight only lasted 3 minutes and reached max altitude of 30 ft. No other issues were seen and will not be flying outdoors anymore from home without authorization.
ASRSN:2112848.s: A pilot operated a new DJI Mini 3 drone from home into Class B airspace, reaching 30 feet for three minutes. The pilot realized they were not under the Class B shelf as assumed and stated they will not fly outdoors from home without authorization.

ASRSN:2112881.n: While parked at the gate, a passenger came to the flight deck and said he was an FAA inspector. I didn't see any credentials. He said while we were on approach, approximately four miles from landing on Runway 13L, he observed a drone underneath us. Neither Pilot saw the drone. The weather at the time was mixed IMC and we were on an ILS approach. The passenger was sure he saw something so that's why we are submitting a Safety Report.
ASRSN:2112881.s: A passenger claiming to be an FAA inspector reported seeing a drone under the aircraft during an ILS approach in mixed IMC, four miles from Runway 13L. Neither pilot observed the drone, and the passenger provided no credentials while the aircraft was parked at the gate.

ASRSN:2112888.n: Instructed to cross Runway 15 and continue J to 19. Another aircraft was also instructed to cross 15 on K into the hold block. We waited for two arrivals and then we were cleared to line up and wait. Several markings on J, old and new made us concerned that we were in the wrong area to hold short but couldn't readily see. After line up and wait, a normal takeoff occurred.Although already listed as a hotspot, this hold short area for 19 is very congested and can be confusing.
ASRSN:2112888.s: Pilots reported confusion while holding short of Runway 19 on taxiway J due to conflicting old and new markings, despite being instructed to cross Runway 15. Although the area is a known hotspot, the crew proceeded with a normal takeoff after clearing the congestion.

ASRSN:2112891.n: On climbout, experienced loud air rushing noise. Leveled off at 10,000 ft. and slowed to 210 kts to assess. Pressurization appeared normal but determined that noise was a Safety of flight issue, ran Diversion Checklist, coordinated with Ops and Flight Attendants, informed Passengers, and returned to ZZZ. Landing weight was 119, well under max landing weight. Mechanics found hole in a window seal. After repairs, we departed for ZZZ1 with no issues. Note: This was a rushing air sound and not the whistling noise normally indicative of a seal leak. Weather was an additive condition, buildups and turbulence. Cause of leak was zip tie that rotated when window was opened. The excess of zip tie poking through the housing, rubbed a hole in seal. Maybe use silicon to hold vent tube in place rather than zip ties.
ASRSN:2112891.s: During climbout, the crew heard a loud air rushing noise caused by a zip tie rubbing a hole in a window seal. They diverted to ZZZ, where mechanics repaired the damage before the aircraft departed for ZZZ1.

ASRSN:2112925.n: On climb-out from [Runway] 22R on the HYLND7 SID at about 1000 ft. AGL we encountered suspected wake turbulence and the aircraft rolled to about 35 degrees of bank. The 'BANK ANGLE' alert came on while we were reducing the bank angle. We were cleared for takeoff Runway 22R out of BOS shortly after a company Airbus. While on the HYLAND7 SID the aircraft quickly banked to about 35 degrees angle of bank at approximately 1000 ft. AGL due to suspected wake turbulence. The aircraft 'bank angle' alert sounded as the PF was reducing angle of bank. The remainder of the climb was uneventful.
ASRSN:2112925.s: The crew of an Airbus departing Runway 22R at BOS encountered suspected wake turbulence from a preceding company Airbus at 1000 ft AGL on the HYLND7 SID. The aircraft rolled to 35 degrees, triggering a bank angle alert, but the climb continued uneventfully after the pilot reduced the bank.

ASRSN:2112937.n: Shortly after takeoff Tower called to tell us we had thick black smoke coming out of both engines. He repeated this at least 3 times as we questioned him further. I [requested priority handling] and requested a return to the ZZZ airport. On takeoff Tower advised us we had thick black smoke coming out of both engines. Queried them multiple times and they confirmed the situation. Decided the best course of action was to land at ZZZ and not press on to ZZZ1 even though we had no indications in the cockpit of fire. Landed on Runway XXL and stopped on runway for trucks to look us over. Taxied to the pad and shut down with no issues.
ASRSN:2112937.s: The pilot reported that shortly after takeoff, Tower advised of thick black smoke from both engines, though no cockpit fire indications existed. The crew returned to ZZZ airport, landed on Runway XXL, and shut down after ground inspection revealed no issues.

ASRSN:2112983.n: On the rollout after landing I noticed the back half of a 777 being towed across the active runway on what appeared to be taxiway 1. It wasn't apparent if the aircraft had a beacon on but he surely did not have any strobes on. I queried ATC about the aircraft on the runway and he said that he was clearing and to not worry about it. The FO and I do not recall hearing any clearance by tower to an aircraft to taxi across the active runway nor did we see them due to the lack of strobes and nighttime conditions. If I saw this aircraft halfway out on the rollout that means the whole body was across the runway during the touchdown. Following conduct of ILS XXR app into ZZZ in night VMC conditions, after safely landing on the runway, and upon rollout vicinity of intersection 1, the CA and FO identified a wide body aircraft taxiing across the end of RWY XXR, appearing to be on intersection 2 northbound. At first identification of the aircraft, it appeared its rear half was still on XXR exiting. The aircraft appeared to have minimal lighting on during its crossing of XXR. Tower was advised of the aircraft identified by the CA as we identified it and they replied that it was exiting now. There was no prior announcement by the tower of the crossing traffic.
ASRSN:2112983.s: The Captain and First Officer of a landing aircraft observed a 777 taxiing across the active runway at night with minimal lighting and no prior Tower clearance. The crew reported that the wide-body aircraft was already crossing the runway during their touchdown, prompting a query to ATC who claimed the aircraft was exiting.

ASRSN:2113012.n: Cleared for takeoff RWY XX in ZZZ from full length Intersection 1. Tower cleared us for takeoff, we pulled out onto RWY and I aligned aircraft with centerline, I straightened aircraft out and rolled straight ahead on centerline. Approximately 2 seconds after alignment on centerline I instructed First Officer, your aircraft", he stated "my aircraft." We brought thrust levers up, paused and then advanced thrust towards takeoff setting. Almost immediately the aircraft had a hard uncommanded yaw to the right. Initially we thought it might have been nose wheel deflection. However, it yawed to the right for unknown reason. When we were approximately 10-15 degrees right of centerline, I called "reject, my aircraft." I performed a long speed rejected takeoff and we informed Tower and notified passengers to remain seated. We exited runway at Taxiway 2 and stopped aircraft. Rejected takeoff items were completed. No immediate danger. Low speed reject. Less than 10kts. QRC procedures were followed but checklist not read. Interrupted by Tower calling. However, we did inadvertently complete all items on all checklist. We taxied 2 engine back to Gate XX and notified Maintenance, Dispatch, and Chief Pilot for debrief. I performed a post flight inspection and found no leaks or damage to nose tire, nose gear, main gear, brakes, engines. No damage or excessive wear found by myself or tech ops. FO and I debriefed before heading to new aircraft. I debriefed and talked with flight attendants on the way to new outbound air aft. All crew verbally stated that they were good to continue. Chief Pilot debriefed via phone." The Captain gave me aircraft control once we were pointed straight down the runway, with the throttles about 30% N1. I pushed them up to around 70% and pressed the TOGA button. Immediately following this, while the power was still coming up and before the check thrust" call the aircraft started to veer to the right. Not dramatically but enough to bring the nose of the aircraft away from centerline. I suspected the wind pushing the tail and tried to correct using full left rudder. The aircraft did not turn back toward the left so I held the throttles where they were somewhere in the middle and applied differential break as a reflex to keep from getting further from centerline. The Captain said "reject, I have the controls" and brought the thrust levers to idle and aircraft to a stop. We estimate we were only moving around 10 knots at the time of reject and the aircraft was about 15 feet right of centerline with a 10-15 degree angle away from it. We asked Tower to taxi off the runway and were able to talk about what happened and come up with a plan to return to the gate. No emergency was declared."
ASRSN:2113012.s: The crew rejected a low-speed takeoff on RWY XX after the aircraft experienced an uncommanded right yaw shortly after thrust advancement. No damage was found during inspection, and the aircraft returned to the gate for debriefing with no emergency declared.

ASRSN:2113015.n: During descent into ZZZ [airport], the L1 windshield suddenly cracked and began arcing. I immediately turned off the L1 windshield heat switch, began to slow to 250 KIAS from the ATC assigned 300 KIAS and asked the FO to inform ATC. I then asked him to run the Window Damage procedure. We ran that procedure to completion and continued inbound to ZZZ. ATC (ZZZ Center) asked if we were declaring an emergency to which I declined. I felt since the airplane was flying normally and this was a crack in the outer pane of the windshield we did not need assistance. Upon check-in with approach, they had [given priority handling] us. The fire trucks were waiting for our arrival. After an uneventful landing we taxied in with the emergency vehicles following.Because of the event, they turned us west on [taxiway] 1 to taxi away from the normal flow of traffic. After we declined inspection by the fire trucks, we were given taxi instruction [taxiway] 2, 3, 4, and 5 to the gate. I misunderstood and taxied [taxiway] 2, 3 thinking we were to go to gate X and join the normal sequence of traffic into the ramp. As we arrived at the gate, ZZZ ground call and provided a phone number for the TRACON. They had a few question about whether there were injuries and the nature of the issue. I spoke to the Ops Manager and answered the questions. The ELB (Electronic Log Book) was entered, maintenance, manager and an Inflight Supervisor met us at the gate. I also made a PA upon arrival to the pax (passengers) to communicate why emergency vehicles had met us and followed us to the gate.
ASRSN:2113015.s: During descent into ZZZ, the L1 windshield cracked and arced, prompting the crew to reduce speed to 250 KIAS and execute the Window Damage procedure. The aircraft landed safely with emergency vehicles present, but the pilot later misunderstood taxi instructions, deviating from the assigned route before reaching the gate.

ASRSN:2113024.n: First officer and I noted oil pressure significantly lower than normal. Was hovering around 34 psi. It stayed steady at 34 psi while I was in the cockpit. While I was on break the oil pressure decreased into the amber band and both copilots notified maintenance /dispatch as well as did a preparatory checklist just in case it continued to drop. once again, it stabilized around 29 to 28 psi. Upon arrival into ZZZ mechanics discovered the oil cap was not secure and oil was leaking from the motor.
ASRSN:2113024.s: The flight crew observed low engine oil pressure dropping to 28–29 psi during the flight. Upon arrival, mechanics found the oil cap was unsecured, causing an oil leak from the engine.

ASRSN:2113029.n: Ramp loaded HAZMAT in pit 1 by itself, unsecured. Ramp then pushed out the aircraft prior to finalizing flight. Aircraft had to return to the gate so Ramp could move HAZMAT to pit 3 to secure dangerous goods.
ASRSN:2113029.s: Ramp personnel loaded unsecured HAZMAT in pit 1 before pushing the aircraft out. The flight returned to the gate so Ramp could move the dangerous goods to pit 3 for proper securing.

ASRSN:2113082.n: On Day 0, 4 different flights, from 4 different stations had to return to the gate because the aircraft was pushed out before the flight was finalized and HAZMAT was unsecured. All 4 had to return to the gate to move the HAZMAT to a different pit location so the dangerous goods could be secured, resulting in a significant inconvenience to our passengers. All were first flight of the day. This is a significant safety issue. This is happening everyday multiple times a day all across our system. We need to do a better job as an airline securing HAZMAT. Below are the flight details. 4 flights reported with unsecured DG (Dangerous Goods) at final. Day 0 Aircraft X ZZZ - ZZZ1. Day 0 Aircraft Y ZZZ2 - ZZZ3. Day 0 Aircraft Z ZZZ1 - ZZZ4. Day 0 Aircraft A ZZZ5 - ZZZ2.
ASRSN:2113082.s: Four first flights of the day from different stations returned to the gate after being pushed out with unsecured HAZMAT. The aircraft had to be repositioned to secure the dangerous goods, causing significant passenger inconvenience and highlighting a systemic safety issue.

ASRSN:2113154.n: While taxiing to gate (approximately 50 ft away), a white van approached the red ramp safety area at the aircraft's 10-11 clock position, stopped briefly at the painted boundary, then continued to within approximately 15 ft in front of the running number one engine. Upon seeing the vehicle enter the safety area, the flight crew stopped the aircraft. The van paused again in front of the engine, then proceeded under the left wing of the aircraft and out of the area. Once the area was again clear, the flight proceeded to the gate without further incident.Van driver not respecting designated safety area nor yielding to moving aircraft. Additional/remedial training for ground vehicle operator.
ASRSN:2113154.s: During taxi to the gate, a white van entered the ramp safety area and approached within 15 feet of the running number one engine, causing the flight crew to stop the aircraft. The incident was attributed to the van driver failing to respect the safety zone and yield to the moving aircraft, prompting a recommendation for additional training.

ASRSN:2113158.n: Runway 05 at ORF is undergoing construction. This was my first time flying into ORF since the construction began. Many of the published approaches to runway 05 were NA and/or out of service due to the construction. This was a night time arrival where the weather had broken ceilings at 5,000 ft and gusty quartering headwinds. Approach gave us direct to CALEY (initial fix for runway 05) to intercept the final for runway 05. To navigate and backup the visual approach, we loaded the RNAV (GPS) M Rwy 5 as noted in the dispatch release stating the approach is available and authorized. We previously accomplished the before landing checklist 'to the line' and only had the 'below the line' items to accomplish as we approached CALEY. As the pilot flying, I became fixated on finding the runway at night after descending through broken cloud layers. The aircraft was configured with gear down and flaps 15 as we approached CALEY. I called for aircraft configuration from flaps 15 to flaps 25 as we navigated passed CALEY to COSTR (final approach fix). I spotted the runway and my attention focused on navigating to the runway to land. I did not call for flaps 30 or 'below the line' on the before landing checklist prior to COSTR because of my focus on lining up to fly a visual to Runway 05. I continued to descend until we received a GPWS warning at approximately 300 feet and immediately executed a go-around. That is when I realized the aircraft was only at flaps 25 and not being fully configured was the reason for receiving the GPWS warning. We accomplished the go-around and climbed to 2,000 feet per ATC instructions. ATC then vectored us to set-up again for a visual to runway 05. That approach led to a fully configured landing on runway 05. Cause: Causal factors that played a role in this event were: 1) My fixation on finding the runway at night. 2) The ceilings at 5,000 feet that made it difficult to find the runway confidently and quickly. 3) Many of the normal lighting features for a runway such as a PAPI and the centerline lights are NOTAM'd out of service due to the construction.Suggestions: My recommendation to prevent this type of event from occurring in the future is to follow the procedures for the before landing checklist to be configured by the final approach fix. My attention on locating the runway took my focus away from finishing aircraft configuration. Even though I had a 2 mile ring around the FAF in the fix page as a reminder to be configured, my attention was mostly outside. I also recommend pilots to consider asking to fly the RNAV (GPS) M Rwy 5 even in visual conditions to be appropriately lined up for the runway, particularly for pilots flying into ORF for the first time since the construction began.
ASRSN:2113158.s: During a night visual approach to Runway 05 at ORF, the pilot flying became fixated on locating the runway and failed to complete the landing checklist, resulting in a GPWS warning at 300 feet. The crew executed a go-around, climbed to 2,000 feet, and subsequently landed safely after fully configuring the aircraft.

ASRSN:2113175.n: On approach into ZZZ a plane not talking with ATC was climbing out of a downtown airport, we responded to an RA and I believe the conflict got with in 100-200 feet of our aircraft.
ASRSN:2113175.s: A pilot on approach to ZZZ reported a conflict with a non-communicating aircraft climbing from a downtown airport. The crew responded to a Resolution Advisory, estimating the separation reduced to 100–200 feet.

ASRSN:2113180.n: I was tasked with flying an aircraft from storage to heavy maintenance. The flight was operated on a ferry permit due to overdue maintenance items. I added several MEL items before we departed. Climbing through around 10,000 feet, we encountered a cloud layer and received an ICE caution message. At approximately 12,000 feet we received a L WSHLD HEAT caution message. I announced that I had the aircraft and the radios, and called for the QRC/QRH checklists. I glanced up to see if the windshield was accumulating ice and noticed a crack running from the bottom of the windshield to the center. I stopped the climb and began slowing. We relayed to ZZZ Center that we had an issue with our windshield and would be stopping the climb and returning to ZZZ. They issued a heading to the airport and told us to report the field in sight. No emergency was declared, and the remainder of the flight continued normally.Upon landing, we discovered the crack had grown in length since first noticed, and a second crack was observed from the center post moving towards the center of the windshield.
ASRSN:2113180.s: The pilot flying a ferry flight encountered ice and windshield heat cautions at 10,000 and 12,000 feet, revealing a windshield crack. After stopping the climb and returning to ZZZ Airport without declaring an emergency, the crack grew and a second crack appeared upon landing.

ASRSN:2113280.n: While flying at FL400 we were advised of a line of storms ahead of us. We turned on our on board weather radar and clearly saw two cells, one to the left of us and one to the right, but there was no weather detected directly ahead of us on our route.We then looked outside and saw the cells to the left and right and saw clouds below us in front of us but it was clear we would be higher than them. As we flew over the clouds we could clearly see past them and see the ground on the other side. At some point over the top of the clouds we started to experience turbulence, then a very strong downdraft that forced the airplane down to FL390 regardless of any action we took. I reported severe turbulence in accordance with AIM 7-1-21 definitions and asked for a block altitude FL390-410 which was granted. Within several seconds we had climbed back to 400 and seemed stable. Then we experienced an updraft and the aircraft climbed to 410. We regained control and were then on the other side of the storm and had an uneventful rest of the flight.
ASRSN:2113280.s: The flight crew encountered severe turbulence and a strong downdraft while flying at FL400 through a storm cell not detected by weather radar. The aircraft was forced down to FL390 before recovering to FL400 and climbing to FL410 due to an updraft, after which the flight continued uneventfully.

ASRSN:2113301.n: My student and I were on a practice IFR flight doing approaches, specifically the RNAV 29 Circle 18. We were 5 NM out on the final approach course, getting ready to circle to Runway 18 when I see a plane off to my right but he was reporting a midfield left downwind when he was actually more of a left base. I communicated with him and asked for his intentions. He kept saying midfield when he just was not. He started turning in towards us to come in behind us but he was just coming in towards us at the same altitude. I had to talk to him again and he still couldn't see us, so I had to take controls from my student because I was the Safety Pilot. We broke off the approach and had to reintercept it back. We had the traffic alert pop up on our MFD (Multi-Function Display), and I had to take evasive action. After he spotted us, he followed us in way too close for my comfort. It felt like tailgating essentially. He was less than 0.5 NM from us the whole time in the pattern all the way to landing.I want to suggest better rules for pattern entry as well as pilots knowing better position reporting capabilities. Auburn is a busy training airport and non-Auburn general aviation pilots tend to not realize how chaotic it can be at times. A lot of traffic conflicts occur with Auburn airplanes and non-Auburn airplanes, and it needs to be addressed.
ASRSN:2113301.s: A flight instructor and student conducting an RNAV 29 approach at Auburn encountered a conflicting aircraft misreporting its position as midfield left downwind while actually on left base. The instructor took control to break off the approach due to the other pilot's failure to see them and subsequent tailgating within 0.5 NM.

ASRSN:2113304.n: I was undertaking a solo cross country flight from ZZZ1 to ZZZ2 in order to continue to build hours in preparation for gaining my Commercial Pilots License.The aircraft preflight all appeared normal. The engine had 6 quarts of oil and the fuel was topped off to full at ZZZ1. During the preflight engine run-up checks the magneto checks were all well within tolerances and there was no unusual engine vibration or roughness observed.Prior to departure from ZZZ1 I picked up VFR flight following from ZZZ Approach. The take-off was uneventful and upon reaching a cruise altitude of 4500 ft. MSL I reduced power and leaned the mixture out to Rich of Peak. Approximately 40 minutes into the flight I was instructed to remain east of the freeway for reported skydiving activity over Lake A by ZZZ Approach, which I complied with. When I was approximately 4 NM east of ZZZ the engine RPMs dropped suddenly to about 2000 RPMs. Some popping noises were heard coming from the engine and I felt significant engine vibration. I [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Approach and told them I was experiencing engine problems and needed to land. I looked for my best landing spot. I Squawked XXXX and ran through my initial flows for power loss in flight. Applied carb heat, checked the fuel position, enriched the mixture full, cycled the throttle and checked the magnetos and primer. I looked over at my emergency checklist to my side and double checked I hadn't missed anything. I decided ZZZ airport was the safest option so proceeded direct to the airport and was switched over to the Unicom frequency for the private airport. I contacted Unicom and told them I was in a left downwind for the north runway and needed to land. They advised me it was a dirt strip, which I was aware of. I proceeded to keep the engine power at idle and make a short approach to ensure I made the runway in the event of complete engine failure. As I assessed I still had some potential engine power available if I really needed it, I elected to keep the engine running as I had no indications of fire. Upon landing I was able to turn around and taxi a short distance before shutting the engine down to prevent possible further damage.After landing the airport manager informed ZZZ Approach I was safely on the ground. I followed up with my own call to ZZZ Approach shortly afterwards to confirm they required no further information from me.Post flight inspection of the engine by a qualified A&P at the airport revealed a bent push rod for the #1 cylinder.
ASRSN:2113304.s: A solo student pilot experienced sudden engine power loss and vibration at 4,500 feet during a cross-country flight due to a bent push rod in cylinder #1. The pilot executed emergency procedures, declared an emergency, and safely landed on a dirt runway at ZZZ airport.

ASRSN:2113305.n: While cruising on autopilot during an IFR flight at FL100, I noticed something shiny approaching fast from the front right of our plane and at the same altitude. The object quickly passed to the right (east) of our position and within 1,000 ft vertically of our right wing. The object's altitude was within 100 ft of ours. My passenger also saw the object.The object was not visible on TCAS/ADS-B and no evasive action was taken. The time from the first sighting to the passing was less than 10 seconds and the object was clearly not going to hit us.The object appeared metallic and shiny. My opinion is that it was a mylar balloon, a weather balloon, or potentially a drone (although it did not appear to have wings and I did not see any propellers). The object was completely shiny and did not have any writing on it. It was too small to be another aircraft, and my guess is that it had a diameter less than five feet.I immediately reported the sighting to Louisville Approach along with my current altitude. Louisville Approach stated that they did not have any targets visible on radar in the vicinity.The remainder of the flight was uneventful. Nothing further to report.
ASRSN:2113305.s: A pilot reported a shiny, metallic object passing within 1,000 feet vertically and 100 feet of altitude during an IFR cruise at FL100. The object, undetected by TCAS or radar, was likely a balloon or drone, and no evasive action was required as the flight continued uneventfully.

ASRSN:2113323.n: Lost aircraft signal while flying way point mission. Probably altitude too low and signal lost when large condo building was between drone and my controller. RTH (Return to Home) on lost signal did not work. The drone never returned. Last know point was over swamp. No damage or injury.
ASRSN:2113323.s: The pilot lost signal with a drone during a waypoint mission, likely due to low altitude and obstruction by a condo building. The Return to Home function failed, leaving the drone unrecovered over a swamp with no damage or injury.

ASRSN:2113339.n: On arrival previous flight, we encountered some airspeed deviations due to wind/temperature but nothing significant. Through flight was normal. Runway 08, the normal runway, was closed. Runway 21 was the only active runway. Weather was clear, calm, altimeter 30.06. V1 126, VR 134, V2 137.Takeoff on Runway 21 run-up and initial acceleration were normal using autothrottle. Engine stabilized at 92.8 reduced N1. Shortly after the V1 call, at 130 kt., abruptly yawed right and the left wing rose significantly. It felt like we had encountered jet wash or wind shear.Corrections were immediately applied to level the wings and maintain runway heading. The anomaly stopped while we assessed blown tire and possible loss of an engine, neither of which were indicated. Takeoff roll continued. No further adverse indications were encountered, rotation and the remainder of the takeoff were normal. All aircraft systems were assessed and appeared to be normal. Flight was continued to ZZZ. Passengers and flight attendants were notified of the event and given an explanation. Albuquerque Tower was informed of the anomaly. The remainder of the flight and landing in ZZZ were uneventful. Post-flight inspection was performed and nothing unusual was noted.Given the weather conditions in ABQ, and the lack of any significant winds, I suspect we encountered jet blast from some type of engine run from either Aircraft Y or the Aircraft Z stationed to the west of Runway 21.
ASRSN:2113339.s: The flight crew experienced an abrupt right yaw and left wing rise shortly after V1 during takeoff on Runway 21, suspecting jet blast from nearby aircraft. No system failures were found, the takeoff continued normally, and a post-flight inspection revealed no anomalies.

ASRSN:2113350.n: The review team concluded a report that I had filled for a TCAS RA during a visual approach into BUR with Aircraft Y, that required evasive action the night of Day 0. I had another near collision event with multiple aircraft departing BUR in day VMC conditions. I was pilot flying (PF) and we had departed Runway 15 on the OROSZ2 Departure with LNAV/VNAV CMD A ON SQUAK of XXXX, we were honoring sterile cockpit procedures. I had the window open with 210 kts. in order to expedite our climb, which is always my plan to reduce the threat of general aviation traffic conflicts and gain altitude to receive a turn north with ATC. However, for some reason ATC was not issuing a turn clearance for some time. I remember thinking how unusual it was to have a clear view of LAX, as we were approximately 10 to 15 miles southwest of BUR, before ATC issued a turn to a 360 heading. We began the turn and were climbing through 6,000', when ATC issued a Traffic Alert of a general aviation aircraft at 11 o clock at 6,500' and to expedite our turn." I ensured the aircraft was turning at the maximum 30-degree standard rate turn while we attempted to acquire the traffic visually. ATC then changed their mind and recommended we level off, which I promptly hit ALT HLD on the Mode Control Panel (MCP). However, due to our climb rate, the automation stopped our climb at 6,400'. ATC then issued another clearance to a fix. We continued our turn away from the traffic and additional clearance to a higher altitude was directed. To my surprise, ATC then issued another traffic conflict at our 12 o'clock position and above our altitude. I saw the target on TCAS. I believed Safety of Flight to be in question. Our closure rate, distance and altitude presented a significant collision hazard and I only had moments to take immediate action. I made the decision to not rely on last second ATC instructions or wait for a potential TCAS escape guidance and instead took immediate action to avoid a potential collision. I disengaged all automation and aggressively pitched the aircraft to 20-degrees of pitch and added near maximum thrust. As the nose of the aircraft pitched above the aircraft, I lost visual contact of the aircraft. No TCAS Alerts or RAs resulted and when it appeared we were clear of the aircraft I resumed normal operations and the rest of the flight was uneventful. No deviations from ATC clearances were apparent and ATC did not raise any concern.Preventative Measures: The First Officer (FO) and I debriefed the event later. We believed it unreasonable for ATC to direct many conflicting clearances and amendments to instructions to a transport category airline turbojet. We simply cannot maneuver to the extent ATC was expecting. We questioned why ATC had delayed our turn after departure and especially why ATC turned us towards two aircraft. It's our synopsis in this day and age with ADSB technology in general aviation aircraft that ATC knows the position of these aircraft and while their primary duty is to separate IFR from IFR traffic changes need to be made to improve safety in SoCal's procedures and or airspace parameters."
ASRSN:2113350.s: The Pilot Flying reported a near collision while departing BUR in Aircraft Y, where conflicting ATC clearances directed the jet toward two general aviation aircraft. The pilot disengaged automation and aggressively pitched up to avoid a collision, noting that ATC failed to account for the transport jet's maneuvering limitations.

ASRSN:2113352.n: At about 20 to 25 minutes into the flight, the aircraft was in the process of leveling off at flight level 340 with the autopilot engaged. There was just a little bit of light chop, seat belt sign was on, the flight attendants were up. As the aircraft started the level-off it rolled aggressively about 30 to 35° to the right and pitched up what I believe was around 5 to 7°. I immediately grabbed the controls and started the recovery maneuver, push roll thrust stabilize. The aircraft rolled several times, each time I had to do the recovery maneuver. For a second I thought that I had a flight control problem because the flight controls weren't responding the way I was expecting due to the rolling action of the wake. Once stabilized at FL340 we advised ATC that we think we encountered wake turbulence. The controller's response was, 'Yeah there was a heavy Airbus up there. Contact Washington Center.' I called the flight attendants and asked how they were and if there was any damage or injury. They said they were OK and just some spilled drinks in the galley.
ASRSN:2113352.s: The pilot encountered wake turbulence from a heavy Airbus while leveling off at FL340, causing aggressive rolling and pitching. The pilot manually recovered the aircraft, and although no injuries occurred, some drinks were spilled in the galley.

ASRSN:2113376.n: ZZZ ZZZZ pilot monitoring (PM) left seat, pilot flying (PF) Right seat. Wx 140/17G23kts 1200BKN 5BR. We elected to use the new wind procedure and discussed it in our threat brief in the briefing area before walking to the jet. Our acft had a distractor, a previous writeup from ZZZ1 which was addressed was about door 1L. The door light would illuminate on the EICAS. We did see it twice only briefly on the taxi out, in each case as quick as it was up on the EICAS it went away. We added to the threat brief that if we saw the light on takeoff roll we would not reject for it. If it stayed on airborne we would then obviously have to address it. We used the software's optimized flap solution and delayed rotation to VR max which was VR+20. Rotation was on the slower side and winds were gusting but down the runway for the most part. Acft weight was 197,000 and runway takeoff data was for 199,000. We discussed the threat of being light and the max thrust for takeoff, which resulted in a slower rotation. Pos Rate gear up came quick and 800 ft was just as quick. We were at V2+25-30 so fast. As soon as PF called for VNAV and I executed the command the engine starting popping and wooshing sound. To the simulators benefit it was very close to the sim experience. So we have a V2 cut, the PF due to the yawing at first thought we had a engine seizure, the popping and having previous experience with Compressor stall. After announcing a Compressor stall we disconnected the autothrottles (AT) and retarded the L Eng to idle. As soon as the engine was pulled back the Comp stall ceased and the engine recovered. Talk about the law of primacy, I did grab the card first before accessing my EFB. Right after the retarding the throttle I [requested priority handling] told Tower we were going straight out and to Stby. At the same time the PF called for VS 100 climb airspeed and AT Arm switch off (which is was). With the Eng stabilized we went to follow the checklist, Gear off, flaps being retracted on speed which was happening quick. At climb airspeed, FL CH, airspeed max con and we were already at or close to 4000 ft. Step 7 had us advance the thrust lever slowly and check that EGT and RPM would follow, they did perfectly. We elected to run the Eng at idle and that we could use it for a GA if necessary. So this is where the checklist could be confusing, step 8 was satisfied as normal then go to 13. We elected to say eng runs at a reduced thrust or idle thrust. I would not want a crew to recover compressor stall and think about continuing. I could see that being slightly confusing. We completed the checklist and the hyperlinks were amazing, hitting the Non Normal config with a landing distance came so fast I thought I might of missed something. I actually referenced it again to make sure I had looked up the correct data, I came up with the same results. We were taking vectors at 4000 ft for the ILS XX. When we input the divert to ZZZ an ACARS prompt appeared to notify Dispatch. I sent a quick dispatch msg with a reply do you need equipment……a distractor that we should streamline. I would like to see that added to the initial prompt we received which was handy and efficient. We briefed the Flight Attendant (FA) via the PA and worked on FMC cleanup. The PF continued and on downwind we were ready for base leg to final, one thing I don't recall is did we request landing data, we might of missed that step. Flaps 20 and GS intercept the PM left the Autopilot on till we broke out. Gusty winds were from 120-140 deg was noticeably present. touchdown and rollout were normal maybe slightly long with late thrust reduction and F20. A missed opportunity for the threat fwd brief as a known result of F20. One critique I had for the PF was thrust reverse were stowed at 80kts, The result was brakes at 3s the 4s. Fire trucks were present and the chief reached out to see if we needed anything and we replied negative. At the appropriate time we shut down the motor and taxied uneventfully to the gate with fire trucks following.
ASRSN:2113376.s: The pilot monitoring reported a left engine compressor stall shortly after takeoff in gusty winds, caused by rapid VNAV engagement. The crew recovered the engine by retarding the throttle, diverted to an alternate airport, and landed safely with fire trucks following.

ASRSN:2113415.n: Taxiing to the gate we were given hold short of [Runway] XR on north side of the runway. We were there for 15 minutes waiting for the alley to clear. We shut down engine 2 to conserve fuel. There was an aircraft on a 2 mile final. The controller called us to give clearance to cross. The first transmission was blocked by another aircraft. We got the second transmission and started to cross. The aircraft took a second to start rolling with one engine. We were across the hold short line when the controller told us to stop because we were going to slow. I radioed back that we will stop but are across the hold short line. The controller then sent the aircraft on short final around. They told us to continue crossing. We proceeded to the gate after crossing without further issue. Holding short, runway XR, air traffic control cleared us to cross, but the transmission was blocked, so she cleared us to cross again, (single engine taxi), as we were about one aircraft link past the hold short line she told us to 'stop, because we weren't moving' (yes, you certainly were). We told Controller we had already crossed the line, so then Controller gave us clearance to cross again and told the other aircraft to go around.
ASRSN:2113415.s: The crew, taxiing single-engine to the gate, received a blocked clearance to cross Runway XR and began moving before the controller ordered a stop due to slow speed. After the crew confirmed they had already crossed the hold short line, the controller cleared them to continue and instructed an approaching aircraft to go around.

ASRSN:2113421.n: Operating a 777-200 from ZZZZ-ZZZ we had a generally routine flight. We expected and briefed the ILS-XXL approach and were subsequently told to expect Runway XXC and so rebriefed the ILS to that runway. We were cleared the visual approach to XXC and as we approached the airport we observed the preceding arrival land and clear the runway and another aircraft cross at the rollout end. Below 100 ft AGL the Tower broadcast excitedly, Aircraft X GO AROUND traffic on runway!" Without hesitation we executed the go around procedure and as we did so the Tower Controller made a remark that he had received an erroneous indication from his runway-occupied monitoring system and sounded just as surprised as we were at the occurrence. The controller did not issue us go-around instructions and that left us uncertain about whether we should follow the aircraft guidance, which was commanding a right turn in accordance with the ILS missed approach procedure, or continue runway heading. The Tower was also busy directing other traffic so I was unable to clarify our instructions until probably above 1000 ft AGL, and this delay and confusion led to a disruption of standard callouts and procedures. Positive control of flightpath was never in question but the safety margins were definitely reduced due to the lack of clarity of instructions. By the time we leveled at 3000 MSL we had regained the shared mental model and confirmed the aircraft was configured properly, the autoflight matched our desired flightpath and necessary checklists were completed."
ASRSN:2113421.s: A 777-200 crew executing a visual approach to Runway XXC initiated a go-around after the Tower broadcast a traffic warning caused by an erroneous runway-occupied system indication. The controller's failure to issue explicit go-around instructions created confusion regarding the missed approach path, reducing safety margins until positive control was re-established above 1000 ft AGL.

ASRSN:2113424.n: While at cruise at FL340 in IMC FO side airspeed on ADI fails. I point out to Captain and cross checks his side. Receive RUDDER RATIO and MACH TRIM EICAS CAUTIONS. Immediately after CPT airspeed on ADI fails. Preform QRC. I [requested priority handling]. Request FL180. We decide to divert to ZZZ. Captain gives me control of the aircraft and let Flight Attendants (FAs) and Dispatch know what we are doing. Land in ZZZ uneventfully and submitted an ELB report. The flight was delayed for a few hours due to a tail swap. I noticed that weather was starting to build up w of ZZZ1. So I took another look at the filed routing from the initial dispatcher. Around the same time I noticed that ZZZ had posted an advisory for swaps so I refueled him for the most restrictive coded departure route. I planned the crew for a coded departure route that allowed them to get through a whole in the weather nw of ZZZ1. Soon after getting n of ZZZ2 I noticed their tag change to dvrt ZZZ. I messaged the crew and asked them to confirm the diversion and it appeared that they had lost both airspeed indicators and attitude indicators and that they suspected a possible probe ice fail. I knew the severity of the problem, so I initiated the diversion to ZZZ and asked for a debrief on the ground. It sounded as though the weather had built up and they had a lightning strike because he said that soon after they got through the weather, they lost their airspeed indicators and attitude indicators.A few people around me contacted the ops manager and the Maintenance Dispatcher while the diversion was happening. Later I tried to attempt to call ZZZ but no one was picking up and the Ops Manager informed me that ZZZ claimed that they did not have the equipment or staff to support a diversion of a 757. ZZZ is noted as a Regular airport for the 757 and should be equipped to take on a 757 diversion. I can understand that staffing may be limited around XA:30 at night, but they should be equipped to take on this aircraft type.
ASRSN:2113424.s: A Flight Dispatcher coordinated a diversion to ZZZ after a 757 crew lost both airspeed and attitude indicators at FL340, suspecting probe ice failure following a lightning strike. The aircraft landed safely, but the dispatcher noted ZZZ lacked the equipment or staff to support the 757 diversion despite being a regular airport for that type.

ASRSN:2113430.n: I was reassigned to operate XXXX ZZZ-ZZZ1. This was a last minute assignment and boarding was complete before the First Officer (FO) and I arrived. ZZZ Operations boarded the flight without a working PA system, external air or APU air and it got so hot that a passenger had to be removed because they were having a seizure or a stroke (or both). The non working items and heat levels were all noted in the communications, and responded to by ZZZ Operations before boarding began. The passenger was transported to the hospital and did not fly with us yesterday. I was preparing for the flight in the terminal, and following along in chat, and after the medical event with it still hot on board I told ZZZ Operations to deplane the aircraft. When I arrived at the gate, the agent told me that they offered egress and no one wanted to get off. When I went down to the aircraft, I learned that the agents had stopped the Flight Attendants from making an announcement to offer egress. At this point, they had all been on the aircraft for almost an hour, with all but 5 minutes of that time without any type of air circulation, or PA system because the battery was off. Maintenance was walking off the aircraft having started the APU as I arrived. Obviously the heat created a safety issue, and not having a PA available made it very difficult for the Flight Attendant crew to handle the medical problem while boarding was finishing up. As I was starting my aircraft preflight, the agent walked up to me with a phone number for operations, which I called. The operations manager" said that they needed the gate for Aircraft Y from ZZZZ and basically told me to do whatever I could to hurry up. He actually said, I hope you can do what you can at a safe speed to make the gate available, or something like that, but the undertone of the conversation was clear. Separately, I told the agent to deplane the aircraft after the medical problem was removed from the aircraft, and while the flight attendant crew attempted to follow my direction, the gate agent actively defied it, and then lied to my face when I arrived telling me that no one wanted to get off the aircraft. My FO witnessed this, and his recollection was the same. So, with this situation there are a few issues with SOP compliance, safety policy questions, and Captain authority questions.I don't want to live through another XXX, and that's really the way that this situation was headed yesterday. No one on the Airport Customer Service side, or ZZZ Operations seems to care, unfortunately. Seems that there are 3 issues- 1. Operational process to begin and continue boarding under adverse circumstances. 2. Handling of a Medical Event seemingly due to extreme heat and the protection of others exposed. 3. Subversion of Captain's Authority by failing to follow direction to deplane the aircraft due to a safety issue."
ASRSN:2113430.s: The Captain reported that ZZZ Operations boarded a flight without air conditioning or a PA system, causing a passenger medical event and heat exposure. Ground agents defied the Captain's order to deplane the aircraft, prioritizing gate availability over safety and subverting Captain authority.

ASRSN:2113435.n: Aircraft dispatched with [MEL] XXXXX. ICAS showed nose wheel steering 1:45 into flight. Complied with ICAS and Checklist. Notified dispatcher and Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control could be sure if nose wheel steering would work on landing. Coordinated with Chief Pilot. Dispatch advised Person A to have to vehicle standing by. [Priority handling was requested]. Uneventful landing was made. Aircraft was towed to gate. Aircraft dispatched under and compliant with MEL XXXXX. About 1:45 after takeoff and while traversing an area of moderate turbulence, the EICAS Advisory message NOSE WHEEL STEERING and NO LAND 3 appeared simultaneously. Complied with accompanying checklist and contacted Dispatch for a phone patch with Maintenance Control. Maintenance Control was ultimately unable to ascertain whether or not nose wheel steering would be available upon landing. Asked Dispatch to coordinate with ZZZ station to inform ZZZ ATC that we would be a [priority] aircraft for landing with the possibility of being unable to taxi clear of the runway and also to arrange for a tug at the runway to minimize our occupancy of the runway in such case. Upon landing, the nose wheel steering did not work by use of either the rudder pedals or tiller. Aircraft was brought to a near stop straight ahead on the runway and then it was determined that ample steering was available through differential braking to taxi clear of the runway. Ground personnel connected a tug and towed us to gate XXX.
ASRSN:2113435.s: The crew received a nose wheel steering advisory 1:45 after takeoff during moderate turbulence. Although steering failed on landing, the aircraft was safely stopped and taxied clear using differential braking before being towed to the gate.

ASRSN:2113445.n: Frequent 'SPAR VALVE CLOSED' MELs have been placed on multiple Boeing MAX 9 aircraft in the last two days, with two from dispatch alone resulting in a return to gate. Placard number XXXXX/XXXXY/XXXXZ for reference. Aircraft X had a return to gate yesterday, Day 0 at XA:07 as well for the same issue. The Captain of Aircraft X also noted that Aircraft X had a history of the same issue which the Maintenance Controller on duty agreed. While the placard itself does not seem to pose a problem, my concern is that this could potentially be a manufacturing issue or an issue innate in the design of the Boeing MAX 9.
ASRSN:2113445.s: Multiple Boeing MAX 9 aircraft experienced frequent 'SPAR VALVE CLOSED' MELs, causing returns to gate. The reporter suspects a potential manufacturing or design issue, noting Aircraft X has a history of this problem confirmed by the Maintenance Controller.

ASRSN:2113526.n: DISPATCHED SINGLE-PACK (RIGHT PACK INOP). Level @ FL340, both Cabin Pressurization Page and Cruise Page appeared Normal. Approximately 35 nm South of ZZZ1, NNE bound, received clearance from ZZZ Center to climb to FL350. Upon reaching 350, observed CAB V/S indicating 'climb', however, several minutes later CAB V/S still indicated 'climb' and CAB ALT appeared elevated (~>8000). Suspected a malfunction, F/O (Pilot Flying) concurred, advised ZZZ Center we might have a pressurization problem, requested lower altitude, initially given FL240. Shortly thereafter during descent, received EXCESS CAB ALT on/per ECAM. Exercised applicable procedures, [requested priority handling] with ZZZ Center, received clearance to 10,000 ft. Cabin altitude reached maximum of ~11,500 ft, passenger mask not deployed, cockpit crew 02 only. Subsequent to initial decent (~4 minutes), received ECAM CAB PR 1 + 2 FAULT, observed LEFT PACK FAILED/OFF on overhead. Communication with Flight Attendants advised all was well with both passengers and cabin. Weather both enroute and destination was good, plenty of fuel, thus ZZZ2 was suitable and prudent.Single-Pack Operation. Integrity Test of operable Pack Control Valve?
ASRSN:2113526.s: The crew of a single-pack aircraft climbing to FL350 experienced a pressurization failure causing cabin altitude to reach 11,500 ft. They descended to 10,000 ft after receiving an EXCESS CAB ALT warning and a subsequent dual pack fault, landing safely with no passenger mask deployment.

ASRSN:2113552.n: Upon landing in PWM on runway 11, Tower advised us to hurry and make right turn on [taxiway] C because of aircraft on a mile and a half final. There is major construction on taxiway A and C. We had to taxi C to backtrack on runway 36 to make a left on 29 to make a right on D to be able to get to the gate. Being in a hurry as I turn into C, it caught me off guard how narrow C is. I taxied C to B to runway 36 as we do it at other airports. However major concern is anything larger than Aircraft X and also any nighttime operation. I couldn't find any information on minimum taxiway width on FOM nor other materials. I called Dispatcher but no information either as minimum legal taxiway width. I called PWM Tower. He said they are extremely aware of the issue because they have had a couple of aircraft take taxi light out with their gear while making turn C to B to 36. I called for assistance. Told to write a report and called a CP (Chief Pilot). If I had been on anything bigger than Aircraft X I think I would have had to stop and called for a tow bar. There is no reference anywhere other than NOTAMS on closure of the area of [taxiway] A and C. Cause: Taxiway width on C which is not normal route from runway to gates. Suggestions: Research if any messages need to be put out or coordinate with Tower how to get jetliner to gates due to construction.
ASRSN:2113552.s: The pilot of Aircraft X landed at PWM and was directed to taxiway C due to construction, finding the taxiway unexpectedly narrow. The pilot reported that larger aircraft or night operations could risk gear damage, noting Tower awareness of previous incidents and a lack of documented minimum width standards.

ASRSN:2113554.n: After leveling off at FL 320, Aircraft experienced at least 4 audible bangs and yawed. ECAM indication ENG1 STALL appeared twice and disappeared. Flight was inside of 80 miles from ZZZ. Crew [requested priority] and proceeded directly to ZZZ. All applicable checklists were executed. All required notifications were completed. ATC provided vectors to Runway XL at ZZZ. Aircraft cleared runway and was inspected by Airport Rescue and Firefighting before taxiing into the gate. Engine continued to run throughout the evolution.Compressor Stalls caused the crew to divert and land before a potential pending engine failure. Pilots need to maintain situational awareness and always have a plan for where to go in the event of a [failure].
ASRSN:2113554.s: The crew experienced compressor stalls with audible bangs and yaw at FL 320, triggering ENG1 STALL ECAM warnings. They diverted to ZZZ, landed safely on Runway XL, and inspected the aircraft before taxiing to the gate.

ASRSN:2113557.n: Climbing thru FL330 left engine oil pressure went to 1 psi, with associated EICAS indications. All other engine indications normal, except oil temp went from 115 to 85. At first we thought it was just an indicator issue, since there were no other indications. Leveled at fl350 and divided tasks, Captain (me) flew aircraft and worked radios, FO grabbed QRH and did some ACARS coordination. QRH had us questioning which was first decision for Oil Pressure, and when we felt some minor vibration/engine burps we decided it was NOT just an indication, so followed QRH to engine severe damage checklist. Immediately [requested priority handling] and turned back to ZZZ since we were at FL350 and needed to run checklists and descend. All checklists run, jumpseaters briefed and asked for input (none, neither is 767) and Air Turnback sent. ZZZ Crash Fire Rescue (CFR) was there upon arrival, escorted us to Point X. Maintenance met us at the plane and we told him what happened. Climbing through FL330 we got an oil pressure EICAS message, LEFT OIL PRESSURE LIGHT and master caution light. QRH actioned. While diagnosing the problem, a thump was felt. It had the feel of a small compressor stall. SEVERE DAMAGE checklist was then actioned and completed. [Request for priority handling] was made ZZZ Center. Return to ZZZ was deemed most appropriate given our altitude. Landing safely accomplished.
ASRSN:2113557.s: During climb through FL330, the crew experienced left engine oil pressure dropping to 1 psi with a compressor stall thump, prompting a return to ZZZ. They executed the severe damage checklist, received priority handling, and landed safely with Crash Fire Rescue present.

ASRSN:2113606.n: Boarding was complete and we received the ACARS loadout. It stated we had medical goods and dangerous goods in the forward cargo. Asked Operations about it and they sent a Ground worker up to talk. I asked if there was dry ice and biohazard on board. He stated no there are two boxes and no dry ice. I further asked what was in the boxes and he stated a dead animal and body parts. Since this sounded normal, and no dry ice, and no biohazard, I assumed that all was well. Once he stated body parts I should have went and looked myself at that time, but I trusted the worker to do their job but they were trying to do.We departed. After arriving in ZZZ, the FO upon walkaround took a photo of the material in question and it was more boxes (3) and had labeling showing 'type A' and 'radioactive two.' I search our manuals for the labeling 'UN 2915' but came up with nothing more than the many labels that could show up on shipments in the manuals. Also, what I did find was that none of the aforementioned items in this paragraph are allowed in our operations. Incident report filled out and email.Other than verify everyone's job is done and trust that training is lacking, I would make sure scanners and electronic measures are used to confirm items are correctly labeled when scanned in. Could be done with taking images of the scanned item and could derive a legal load.Accepted unnecessary hazard with knowledge of the hazard, failure to properly inspect. Failure to follow procedure by other party, safety concern regarding other party.
ASRSN:2113606.s: The Captain accepted a load containing radioactive body parts after a ground worker incorrectly stated no dry ice or biohazards were present. The crew later discovered prohibited UN 2915 materials, attributing the incident to the worker's procedural failure and the Captain's failure to personally inspect the cargo.

ASRSN:2113607.n: During pushback, tug driver exceeded 90° angle to aircraft and then stopped to pull the aircraft forward to the disconnect point. The driver then appeared to drive forwards towards the nose wheel. At this point, a loud bang was heard and the aircraft was significantly jolted. Tug driver advised they called a Supervisor and then unplugged the headset, hindering our ability to communicate and figure out what happened. Eventually, with the help of ops, we got someone on the headset who advised that the tow bar had broken and the tug made contact with the nose cone of the aircraft. No injuries reported on the ground or on board the aircraft. After some delay in removing the original tug, we were towed back into the gate by a new tug and tow bar. Post flight walk around inspection of the original aircraft revealed damage to the nose cone at the point of contact. We were tail swapped to a new aircraft and continued the flight to ZZZ1 without further issue.
ASRSN:2113607.s: During pushback, a tug driver exceeded the 90° angle, broke the tow bar, and struck the aircraft's nose cone, causing significant jolting and damage. The flight was delayed for repairs, the aircraft was tail-swapped, and the crew continued to ZZZ1 with no injuries reported.

ASRSN:2113707.n: IFR training flight out of RWY 17L PWA received vectors for climb out from TRACON. Level at 4000 feet msl on a heading of 320 we were given a traffic advisory from ATC there was an aircraft was ahead to our 1 o'clock at 3700 feet and 1 mile. I advised ATC we did not have traffic in sight. Several seconds later we received a 'traffic' warning from the G1000 Traffic Information Service indicating traffic was ahead and 500 feet below us. About 3 seconds later when the traffic continued to move closer and when the altitude separation indicated 300 feet I elected to make an immediate left 360 degree turn. Never made visual contact with traffic. ATC queried our turn, we advised them we were making a maneuver for traffic avoidance due to an in-aircraft advisory message. We were told to advise when we could continue with headings. On completion of the 360 degree turn we resumed previous assigned 320 heading and advised ATC we were on course.As the instructor onboard I was concentrating on making sure the student was in compliance with ATC clearances, I could have done a better job of scanning for traffic in VMC and dividing my attention between inside and outside of the aircraft. With the TIS information we had displayed on our MFD I was relatively certain of the other aircraft's position and direction of flight. I believe that a turn away from the aircraft's indicated position as well as the information we received from ATC was the correct course of action as we noted the aircraft getting closer without any further advisories from ATC but had insufficient time to ask ATC for new headings before the in-aircraft advisory was received.
ASRSN:2113707.s: During an IFR training climb at 4,000 feet, the instructor pilot executed a 360-degree left turn after G1000 TIS and ATC advisories indicated conflicting traffic. The maneuver was taken to avoid a collision when visual contact was not established and ATC could not issue new headings in time.

ASRSN:2113730.n: Approaching TUP via the VOR 18 approach during night VMC. Good comms with ATC and Center. Ceiling and visibility good, clear night with moderately strong headwind. No factor. While approaching TUP via this approach, the PAPI lights are on the RIGHT side of the runway. I knew this from route study and the appropriate airport charts. However, this approach has you coming in from the left at an angle. From this angle, there is a set of VERY bright, horizontal white lights that look EXTREMELY similar to the visual indications you would get from the PAPI system. These bright white lights are located on the LEFT side of the runway. This has the potential to create an EXTREMELY dangerous and possibly deadly situation. A task-saturated pilot or inexperienced pilot may target fixate on these white lights on the LEFT side of the runway, unknowingly mistaking them for the PAPI lights. In this case, the 'four white' would indicate being higher than glideslope, causing the pilot to descend. If circumstances aligned and the pilot did not catch this mistake in time, it could easily lead into a Controlled Flight into Terrain situation. This happened in Night VMC, with good view of the ground. It was very jarring to see, but I recognized the situation before any dangerous circumstances happened. I am making this report out of concern for others who may not immediately recognize the situation. I can only imagine how the situation may have been worsened by poor weather conditions, lower ceiling/vis, or lack of experience/situational awareness due to pilot fatigue.
ASRSN:2113730.s: A pilot approaching TUP at night via the VOR 18 approach observed bright white lights on the runway's left side that closely resembled the actual PAPI lights located on the right. The reporter warned that mistaking these lights could cause a pilot to descend below the glideslope, potentially leading to a controlled flight into terrain.

ASRSN:2113739.n: Was providing instruction to new student in an Aeronca Chief. I as the instructor was sitting in the left seat which is the only seat with brakes and the student was in the right seat. We were practicing taxing on the runway as it was a slow day and practicing the skills to control the tail dragger while on the ground. We were practicing brining the tail up and down, one of the most critical phases in controlling a tailwheel plane. The student brought the tail down and the plane instantly turned to the left. I attempted to use right brake/rudder and pulled the power to idle in order to straighten the plane but it was too late and the momentum of the aft CG in the Chief took it left and the plane came in contact with a Runway Feet Remaining sign. The impact with the sign caused damage to the landing gear, wing strut and wooden propeller. The plane has a continental 65hp engine and continental does not have an AD requiring an engine inspection if damage is done to a wooden prop, so the engine remains in good condition. Taildraggers are fundamentally known to be difficult to control on the ground. We were practicing this and the plane became uncontrollable within a matter of a second. By the time I could recognize the plane was headed left my efforts to correct the plane were too late. The biggest contributing factor was the student being new to tailwheel type airplanes and the quickness in which a taildragger can lose controllability.
ASRSN:2113739.s: An instructor and student in an Aeronca Chief damaged the landing gear, wing strut, and wooden propeller while practicing ground handling on a runway. The student lowered the tail, causing an uncontrollable left turn that struck a sign due to the aircraft's aft center of gravity and the student's inexperience.

ASRSN:2113741.n: It has been brought to my attention that I operated at this location without obtaining the correct permission, In future I will apply for FAA LAANC in addition to vendor approval.Day 0 XA:09 PM EDT (30 minute duration)Permissible altitude for authorization: 400 ft.LAANC:Auto approval available up to 400 ft.
ASRSN:2113741.s: The pilot operated a drone without obtaining correct permission, exceeding the required FAA LAANC and vendor approval. The incident occurred at 09:00 PM EDT with a permissible altitude of 400 feet, where auto-approval was available.

ASRSN:2113742.n: It has been brought to my attention that I operated at this location without obtaining the correct permission, In future I will apply for FAA LAANC in addition to vendor approval.Day 0 XA:00 AM EDT (1 day duration)Permissible altitude for authorization: 400 ft.LAANC:Auto approval available up to 400 ft.Airports:ZZZ, ZZZ1
ASRSN:2113742.s: The pilot operated a drone at airports ZZZ and ZZZ1 without obtaining correct permission, exceeding the 400 ft LAANC auto-approval limit. The reporter plans to apply for FAA LAANC and vendor approval in the future to ensure compliance.

ASRSN:2113786.n: OE (Operational Evaluation). I was LCP (Line Check Pilot) / PM. ZZZ approach cleared us to descend from 10K to 7K feet. Later controller asked us to expedite descent and within seconds, we received a TCAS traffic alert (TA). Controller then gave us a turn to heading 070. As we were initiating turn and looking for traffic alert, we received TCAS resolution advisory (RA) to descend. It appeared intrusion aircraft on TCAS was within 200 to 300 feet and climbing. PF (OE Pilot) immediately turned off AP (autopilot) and AT (autothrottles), continuing turn and initiated descent below intrusion zone. I advised controller of TCAS RA descending. The controller acknowledged and within a few seconds, told us we were clear of traffic as well as the aircraft TCAS. Was given another heading and to maintain 7K feet.
ASRSN:2113786.s: During an OE approach, the LCP/PM and PF received a TCAS RA while descending from 10,000 to 7,000 feet after a controller requested an expedited descent. The PF disengaged autopilot and autothrottles to descend below the climbing intruder, after which the controller confirmed the aircraft were clear of traffic.

ASRSN:2113799.n: On the river visual to rwy 19, we received a terrain, pull up" message while on the approach. I was slightly above VNAV flight director guidance, and slightly right of LNAV course guidance. I was erring west to ensure avoidance of prohibited area P56A/B."
ASRSN:2113799.s: The pilot received a "terrain, pull up" alert during a visual approach to runway 19 while slightly above VNAV and right of LNAV guidance. The deviation was intentional to avoid prohibited area P56A/B.

ASRSN:2113802.n: Flying DEN to ZZZ1. Between Gallop and ZZZ1 we lost one and then both GPS receivers. We reported this to ATC who acknowledged. They stated the military does GPS jamming in the area and that could be what the cause was. We reported the incident to dispatch as well. This is the second time in a year that the military jammed not just our GPS, but all traffic in the area as reported by others.
ASRSN:2113802.s: A DEN to ZZZ1 flight lost both GPS receivers between Gallop and ZZZ1. ATC attributed the failure to military GPS jamming in the area, noting this was the second such incident affecting all traffic in the region within a year.

ASRSN:2113813.n: Taxiing out to Runway 20 at night for takeoff. Waiting for arrival traffic to land Runway 2. Sitting short of a runway/taxiway when we noticed ahead there were what appeared to be 2 cars parked right on the edge of the runway. About 500 south of the runway displaced threshold on the west side. No lights on at all on the cars and no beacons. Turned on my lights to confirm. And just as I was asking Tower about these vehicles another aircraft landed on Runway 2 and rolled out sufficiently to come abeam these vehicles. After Tower was queried the vehicles were moved from that location to the infield on the west taxiway. We were subsequently cleared to back taxi into position and then take off. But as we passed that location on the runway for takeoff, our lights revealed that they still had what appeared to be a concrete saw (large one on wheels) sitting just a few feet off the runway edge. These guys had been out there grinding concrete in the middle of the night just off the edge of the runway with cars parked right there 3 feet away from an active runway. And the only reason they moved is because we called them out on it. Additionally. The west taxiway north of the Tango Taxiway is now fresh asphalt, but there are no stripes and only blue edge lights. The whole airport is dark and dank. west taxiway south of Taxiway U has also deteriorated to the point I would not taxi again on it. Huge potholes and broken asphalt. It's so dark you don't see it till you are right on top of it. This is all very dangerous. And impossible to see. The vehicles and equipment had me so rattled I just about refused the whole operation. Unbelievable.
ASRSN:2113813.s: The pilot reported unlit vehicles and a concrete saw parked dangerously close to an active runway at night while taxiing for takeoff. Tower moved the vehicles only after the pilot queried them, but the equipment remained near the edge, and the pilot also cited poor taxiway lighting and surface conditions as hazardous.

ASRSN:2113825.n: During pushback the strap holding the nose gear to the lifting tug came off releasing the aircraft. Maintenance was called to visually inspect the nose wheel and no damage was found.
ASRSN:2113825.s: During pushback, the strap securing the nose gear to the lifting tug detached, releasing the aircraft. Maintenance inspected the nose wheel and found no damage.

ASRSN:2113846.n: After departure from Runway XXL from ZZZ, climbing through FL200, Flight Attendant informed flight deck of an observed mist coming out from under the left wing. Flight Attendant was given FO's IPad and asked him to take a video of what he was observing. After review of the video, we decided to return to ZZZ. We coordinated with Dispatch, ATC, and Maintenance and returned and landed uneventfully back to ZZZ. During flight back to ZZZ, ATC informed us TRACON had [requested priority handling] on our behalf. Normal taxi to gate. Aircraft met by maintenance personnel who were briefed on event.
ASRSN:2113846.s: During climb through FL200 after departing ZZZ, a flight attendant reported mist under the left wing, prompting the crew to return. The aircraft landed uneventfully at ZZZ with priority handling, where maintenance personnel were briefed on the observation.

ASRSN:2113856.n: Ramp did not secure dangerous goods in cargo pit 4, closed the cargo pit doors, and pushed the aircraft out of blocks prior to attempting closeout. Upon inspection of the closeout attempt, it was determined the ramp lead did not secure the item containing dangerous goods per the standard of operations procedures. Aircraft was prompted to return to the gate, causing a significant departure delay.
ASRSN:2113856.s: Ramp personnel failed to secure dangerous goods in cargo pit 4 before closing doors and pushing the aircraft out. The aircraft returned to the gate after the ramp lead was found to have violated standard operating procedures, causing a significant departure delay.

ASRSN:2113860.n: While working aircraft X, I scanned on my dangerous goods to pit 5. With out my knowledge, 3 minutes later the item was held off. I at no point held off any items while working this flight. I never got a verify hold off notice at close out as well.
ASRSN:2113860.s: A mechanic working aircraft X scanned dangerous goods to pit 5, but the item was held off three minutes later without their knowledge or action. The mechanic reported never receiving a verify hold-off notice at close out.

ASRSN:2113895.n: The scooter was held off from being loaded on the aircraft. Smoke was reported to be coming from the panel where the key is inserted to turn on the equipment. The scooter was taken to the baggage service office at ZZZ to be held until the passenger returns from ZZZ1. I was not at the gate to witness the incident. I was briefly made aware of it when I saw it being brought to the baggage service office at ZZZ. I am unsure if any other employee has filed a report and I wanted to ensure it was looked at officially.
ASRSN:2113895.s: A ground employee reported that a passenger scooter was withheld from loading due to smoke emanating from its key panel. The equipment was secured at the ZZZ baggage service office pending the passenger's return from ZZZ1, though the reporter did not witness the incident firsthand.

ASRSN:2113927.n: After landing on Runway XXL and taxiing off the runway normally onto taxiway 1 for the ramp at a taxi speed of about 10 MPH, the aircraft swerved to the left and got a 'Steering Inop' message on the EICAS. The Captain was able to stop the aircraft using heavy braking avoiding the grass area. Ran the QRH after disengaging the steering. After that, the Captain was able to re-engage the tiller and taxi to the gate. Maintenance advised that the aircraft had a history of same malfunction. After landing on Runway XXL taxi off the runway normally on taxiway 1 after taxing straight for about 5 minutes the aircraft swerved to left and got a steering inop EICAS message steering inop was able to stop using heavy braking avoiding the grass areas. Ran the QRH after disengaging the steering try to used the tiler which engaged the steering and was able to text to the gate with caution. After talking to maintenance I was advised that the aircraft has had a history of the same malfunction. Our taxi speed at the time was less than 10 MPH.
ASRSN:2113927.s: The Captain reported a nosewheel steering failure with an EICAS message while taxiing at 10 MPH after landing on Runway XXL. The aircraft swerved left but was stopped using heavy braking; after following the QRH, steering was re-engaged to taxi to the gate, though maintenance noted a history of this malfunction.

ASRSN:2113928.n: On final for Runway 8R tower cleared us to land and cleared an aircraft to cross the runway. Tower later told the aircraft to cancel crossing instructions and hold position. Aircraft Y informed tower the aircraft crossed the holding line. Tower told Aircraft Y to continue crossing, after which tower told us to go around. Tower cleared us to 7000ft and had us on a long vector. Captain inform tower we were close to min fuel, tower acknowledged, Captain later declared min fuel, tower acknowledge, however kept us on a vector away from the airport. Captain make additional call to Approach on our min fuel, they acknowledge with a promise to turn us in soon.
